questions.q: What was the genuinely new term Maxwell added to the existing laws of electromagnetism?
options: Faraday's law — that a changing magnetic field creates an electric field
The displacement current — that a changing electric field, even with no current flowing, creates a magnetic field
Gauss's law for magnetism — that magnetic poles always come in pairs
Ohm's law — that current is proportional to voltage
questions.explanation: Faraday's law and the two Gauss laws were already known from experiment. Maxwell's new contribution, in the Ampere-Maxwell law, was the displacement current: a changing electric field by itself generates a magnetic field. This is what lets the two fields regenerate each other and self-sustain as a wave.

questions.q: Explain why a Maxwellian electromagnetic wave can travel through a perfect vacuum with no medium.
options: It is carried by the luminiferous aether that fills all of space
A changing electric field creates a magnetic field, which (also changing) creates an electric field, each continually regenerating the other
Air molecules pass the vibration along like a sound wave
The wave is pushed forward by the pressure of light's amplitude
questions.explanation: The two fields hold each other up: each changing field constantly recreates its partner, so the disturbance is self-sustaining and needs no air, water, or aether. Maxwell's prediction of waves in nothing at all was exactly what offended the aether-believers of his day.

questions.q: Maxwell calculated the speed of an electromagnetic wave from which two laboratory-measured constants?
options: The charge and the mass of the electron
The permittivity of free space and the permeability of free space
The frequency and the wavelength of visible light
The inductance and capacitance of a Leyden jar
questions.explanation: Maxwell's result was that the wave speed equals one divided by the square root of the permittivity multiplied by the permeability of free space. Both constants had been measured in unrelated experiments on charged jars and current-carrying coils — yet together they gave the speed of light.

questions.q: Why was the match between Maxwell's calculated speed (~310,000 km/s) and the measured speed of light (~300,000 km/s) so significant?
options: It proved light must actually travel much slower than thought
The speed came from electric and magnetic constants having nothing to do with optics, yet equalled the speed of light — implying light is an electromagnetic wave
It proved light is made of particles
It showed light needs a medium to travel
questions.explanation: The speed emerged from constants measured in electrical experiments unrelated to light, yet matched the measured speed of light to within a percent or two. That could not be coincidence: light must be an electromagnetic wave, and an invisible spectrum of other frequencies must exist.

questions.q: In Hertz's apparatus, how did the spark-gap oscillator (the transmitter) produce electromagnetic waves?
options: By heating a wire until it glowed
By making charge oscillate rapidly back and forth along the rods, so the accelerating charge radiates electromagnetic waves
By rotating a magnet near a coil
By passing a steady direct current through a long wire
questions.explanation: When the spark jumped the gap, the stored charge surged back and forth along the rods millions of times per second. Each oscillation is an accelerating charge, and Maxwell's theory says accelerating charges radiate electromagnetic waves — so the transmitter flung a wave into the room with every spark.

questions.q: What physical principle explains how Hertz's loop-antenna receiver detected the waves?
options: The receiver was wired to a hidden battery
Faraday's law — the wave's changing magnetic field through the loop induces a voltage that drives a spark across the gap
Radiation pressure physically pushed electrons across the gap
Heat from the transmitter warmed the loop until it sparked
questions.explanation: The receiver had no power source. As the wave's oscillating magnetic field passed through the area of the loop, the changing flux induced a voltage around the loop (Faraday's law), and at resonance that voltage built up just enough to push a tiny spark across the micrometer gap.

questions.q: From memory, describe how Hertz used a standing wave to measure the wavelength of his invisible waves.
keyPoints: He placed a zinc reflector across the room, so the outgoing wave and the reflected wave overlapped travelling in opposite directions.
The two waves form a standing wave with fixed nodes (always cancel, spark dies) and antinodes (always add, spark brightest).
He walked his detector loop through the pattern and marked the dead spots; the distance between adjacent nodes is exactly half a wavelength.
questions.explanation: If you recalled reflection producing two opposed waves, the node/antinode pattern, and node-spacing = half a wavelength, grade yourself Good or Easy. Timing the wave directly is hopeless — the trick is interference.

questions.q: From memory, name the properties of light that Hertz demonstrated his invisible waves also possessed, proving they were light.
keyPoints: Reflection — bounced off a large zinc sheet like light off a mirror.
Refraction — bent their path through a large prism of solid pitch (asphalt).
Polarisation — rotating the loop to a certain orientation killed the spark, which only happens for a transverse wave.
They also weakened with distance and travelled at roughly the speed of light.
questions.explanation: Mark yourself on how many of reflection, refraction, polarisation (and interference / speed) you recalled. It was the whole package together, not any single measurement, that nailed the case that these waves were light.

questions.q: Hertz found adjacent nodes in his standing-wave pattern spaced about 2 m apart. What wavelength does this correspond to?
questions.given: node-to-node spacing = 2 m;  node spacing = half a wavelength
questions.explanation: The distance between adjacent nodes is half a wavelength, so the wavelength is twice the node spacing. This matches the roughly four-metre wavelength Hertz measured for his waves.

questions.q: Hertz measured a wavelength of about 4 m and calculated the oscillator frequency as about 7.5 x 10^7 Hz. Use v = fλ to find the wave speed, and state why this vindicated Maxwell.
working: This is the speed of light — the same value Maxwell got from \(1/\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}\) two decades earlier.
questions.explanation: Using the universal wave relation v = fλ with the directly measured wavelength and the calculated frequency gives about 3 x 10^8 m/s — the speed of light. Confirming that Maxwell's invisible waves travel at c is the crown jewel that closed the case.
